opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the first thing to say is that "memorize after seeing it once" sounds more magical than it is, and how surprising it is depends on how you define memorization.

The definition I like is roughly extractability. If I give the model some prefix from its training data and it completes the rest verbatim, and the continuation is long and specific enough that it couldn't plausibly have gotten there by chance or general knowledge, then that string is in the model in a meaningful sense. Under that definition, yes, you can find examples that appear to have been seen very few times, sometimes possibly once, that come back out word for word.

But I'd add a few caveats. One is that "seen once" is surprisingly hard to verify. Training sets are enormous and full of near-duplicates. Something that looks unique may appear in slightly different forms dozens of times across scraped copies, mirrors, and forum quotes. So many apparent single-exposure cases turn out to be duplication you didn't find.

The second caveat is that what's memorized usually isn't random. A model that already knows English, code conventions, and the structure of licenses or email signatures only needs to store the surprising bits. Most of a "memorized" passage is predictable given its context, so the model is storing something much smaller than the raw string. That makes one-shot retention much less mysterious: a gradient step on a sequence where a few tokens are really surprising can shift the weights enough that next time, those tokens become the likely prediction.

Third, scale matters a lot. Bigger models memorize more, and faster. We saw this pretty consistently: as you increase parameters, the fraction of training data you can extract goes up, and the amount of repetition needed goes down. So if you'd asked whether a small model memorizes things it saw once, the answer is basically no. For a frontier-scale model, it's much more plausible that some things stick after very little exposure.

Why does this matter? Mostly privacy and security. If memorization only happened for things repeated thousands of times, you could say that's essentially public information. If rare, possibly single-occurrence data can be regurgitated, like someone's phone number in one random document, then deduplication alone doesn't fully solve the problem. That's part of why I think things like differential privacy, or at least careful auditing of what can be extracted, matter, even though they're expensive.

So my summary is: it's real, it's often overstated in individual anecdotes because duplicates are hard to rule out, and it gets more real as models get bigger.

r005.rationale: It offers explanations for memorization, including predictable context and surprising tokens, but does not acknowledge that why some strings are memorized rather than others remains unexplained.

fable-5.1.text:
So the first thing I'd say is that you have to be careful about what "memorize" actually means, because people use the word in ways that are much stronger than the evidence supports.

When we say a model memorized something, the operational definition I like is extraction: can I prompt the model in some reasonable way and get it to emit that string verbatim? That's a behavioral claim about the model, not a claim about what's happening inside it. And when you phrase it that way, the "seen once" claims become more nuanced.

Here's the thing. If I show a model a random 64-character string of hex digits exactly once, and then the model can produce it back, that is genuinely surprising and genuinely interesting. There's no other way the model could have gotten that string except by storing it from that one example. And we do see this happen, particularly with larger models and particularly later in training when the learning rate is low and the model is kind of fine-tuning on everything it sees.

But most of the headline examples aren't like that. If someone says "the model saw this news article once and memorized it," the first question I ask is: did it actually see it once? Because the web is full of duplication. The same article gets syndicated, quoted, scraped into five different datasets, pasted into forums. So when a model regurgitates a paragraph, the honest answer is usually that it saw it dozens of times and the dataset just wasn't deduplicated well enough to know that. We did a lot of work on this. Deduplication reduces memorization a lot, which tells you that repetition is doing a lot of the work.

The second thing is that "memorized" and "could have generated anyway" blur together for natural text. If the model emits the first line of a famous poem, it hasn't necessarily memorized your particular copy. It has learned a distribution in which that sequence is extremely likely. So the counting of exposures gets really muddy for anything that isn't effectively random.

Where the single-exposure claim gets interesting is the regime of rare, high-entropy sequences. Things like API keys, phone numbers, unusual personal details. We have evidence that those can be extracted after a very small number of exposures, sometimes one, and the rate goes up with model scale. That's the thing that actually matters from a privacy standpoint. Nobody cares if the model memorized the Gettysburg Address. People care if it memorized a line from their medical record that was in the training set exactly once.

So my honest summary is: it is possible, it's more likely than people used to think, it grows with model size, but when you see the claim in the wild you should ask whether the data was deduplicated, whether the string is actually unpredictable, and whether anyone actually checked the training data count rather than just assuming.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to be careful about what you mean by “memorize” there. One claim is that a model can see a particular string once during training and then, under the right circumstances, reproduce it exactly. That can happen. But that’s very different from saying the model remembers everything it sees once, or that you can reliably ask it to give that information back.

And “once” refers to the exact string, which isn’t necessarily the same as seeing the information once. If a sentence contains something the model has already learned from many other examples, reproducing that sentence is much less surprising than reproducing a long, random sequence of characters.

The experiment I’d want is to insert a random string into training exactly once, give the model some prefix, and see whether it can recover the rest. Then I’d want to know how often that works, across different strings and different training conditions. A successful example establishes that single-exposure memorization is possible. It doesn’t, by itself, tell you how common it is.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to be a little careful about what you mean by “memorize.” One claim is that seeing a string once changes the model in a way that makes that string more likely. Another, much stronger claim is that you can give the model the beginning of that string and have it reproduce the rest exactly. Those are different things.

And it depends enormously on the string. If it’s something very predictable, reproducing it doesn’t tell you much about whether the model remembered that particular training example. If it’s a long sequence of random characters, then reproducing it is much stronger evidence. You also have to ask whether it really appeared only once, or whether there were duplicates or related examples elsewhere in the training data.

So I wouldn’t interpret “models can memorize something they see once” as “models remember everything they see once.” The interesting question is under what conditions a single exposure leads to something you can actually extract, and how often that happens.

r005.rationale: It asks which conditions make single-exposure strings extractable, but does not acknowledge that the reasons models memorize some strings rather than others remain unexplained.
